title: Find the Last Marked Nodes in Tree
statement:
The tree here is undirected, with `n = edges.length + 1` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1`; each `edges[i] = [u, v]` is an edge between `u` and `v`. Picture a process that marks node `i` alone at time 0. Then, second by second, the marking spreads: every node joined by an edge to an already-marked node becomes marked too, all at the same moment, until no node is left unmarked.

For every start `i`, report a node that is among the last to be marked when the process begins at `i`. Return these as an array `nodes` of length `n`, where `nodes[i]` belongs to start `i`. When several nodes are marked in the final second, any of them is accepted.
notes:
## Intuition

The marks spread one edge per second, so node `v` is marked exactly `dist(i, v)` seconds after the start: the last node marked is a node **farthest** from `i`. A search from every node would find them all in O(n²). A classic fact about trees does better: take a diameter (a longest path) with ends `endA` and `endB`; from any node, one of those two ends is at the largest distance. Three depth-first searches are enough.

## Approach

1. Build the adjacency list `graph` from `edges`.
2. `distancesFrom(start)` runs a depth-first search with an explicit `stack`. A node reached for the first time gets its neighbour's distance plus 1; in a tree, that first visit always comes along the only path from `start`.
3. `farthest(dist)` returns the node with the largest distance. Seen from node 0, it is one end of a diameter: `endA`.
4. Distances from `endA` give `distA`, whose farthest node is the other end, `endB`; distances from it give `distB`.
5. For each node `i`, answer `endA` if `distA[i] > distB[i]`, otherwise `endB`.

## Example 1, step by step

`edges = [[0,1],[0,2]]`. From node 0 the distances are `[0, 1, 1]`, so `endA = 1` (the first of the tied nodes). `distA = [1, 0, 2]` makes `endB = 2`, and `distB = [1, 2, 0]`. Node 0: `1 > 1` is false, so `2`. Node 1: `0 > 2` is false, so `2`. Node 2: `2 > 0`, so `1`. The answer is `[2, 2, 1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): three traversals and one pass over the nodes.
- Space: O(n) for the graph, the distance arrays and the stack.

## Pitfalls

- A search from every node is O(n²), far too slow for 10^5 nodes.
- A recursive search can overflow the call stack on a long path; the explicit `stack` cannot.
- One diameter end is not enough: from nodes near `endA`, the farthest node is `endB`.
- On a tie (`distA[i] === distB[i]`) both ends are marked in the last second, and either is correct.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `graph` | the neighbours of each node |
| `dist` | each node's distance from `start` (-1 until reached) |
| `stack` | nodes reached but not yet expanded |
| `best` | the farthest node found so far in `farthest` |
| `endA`, `endB` | the two ends of a diameter |
| `distA`, `distB` | distances from `endA` and from `endB` |
| `answer` | a last-marked node for each start |
